extracted.intended_audience: college and university administrators, Title IX coordinators, investigators, decision-makers, and institutional counsel responsible for implementing Title IX grievance processes
extracted.subtask_description: Regulatory preamble guidance describing the required elements, limitations, and interpretive rules for recipients' grievance processes under 34 C.F.R. §106.45 (Title IX), including procedural protections, evidence rules, trainings, and duties of Title IX Coordinators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grievance process must comply with §106.45 and apply equally
rubrics_metrics.description: “For the purpose of addressing formal complaints of sexual harassment, a recipient's grievance process must comply with the requirements of this section. Any provisions, rules, or practices other than those required by this section that a recipient adopts ... must apply equally to both parties.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The introductory sentence requires recipients' grievance procedures to meet §106.45's requirements and prohibits adopting asymmetric rules that advantage one party (e.g., cannot provide a hearing only if one party requests it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consolidation of formal complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(4) allows consolidation of formal complaints, in a recipient's discretion, when allegations arise from the same facts or circumstances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consolidation is discretionary and limited to complaints that stem from the same facts/circumstances; recipients should document the factual link before consolidating.

rubrics_metrics.name: No enforcement that requires constitutional violation
rubrics_metrics.description: As acknowledged in §106.6(d), the Department will not enforce these regulations in a manner that requires any recipient to violate the U.S. Constitution, including the First, Fifth and Fourteenth Amendments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are expected to apply grievance processes in ways that avoid violating any party's constitutional rights; preemption and constitutional constraints must be considered in implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rape-shield protections (prior sexual behavior limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The NPRM and final rule incorporate language from the rape shield protections found in Federal Rule of Evidence 412: intended to safeguard complainants against invasion of privacy, potential embarrassment, and stereotyping and to protect complainants 'from being exposed ... to harassing or irrelevant questions concerning their past sexual behavior.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department adopts a broad protection against evidence/questions about a complainant's past sexual behavior unless intrinsically related to the alleged misconduct; see Fed. R. Evid. 412 Advisory Committee Notes for the concept of 'intrinsic' evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition/interpretation of 'prior sexual behavior'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department emphasizes that 'prior' does not imply admissibility of questions or evidence about a complainant's sexual behavior that occurred after the alleged sexual harassment incident, but rather must mean anything 'prior' to conclusion of the grievance process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The phrase 'prior sexual behavior' was chosen because commenters widely understand it to refer to evidence unrelated to the alleged misconduct; aligns with the intent of Fed. R. Evid. 412's prohibition on evidence of a victim's 'other' sexual behavior, but retains flexibility for 'intrinsic' evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties' ability to discuss allegations and gather/present relevant evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients must not restrict the ability of either party to discuss allegations or gather and present relevant evidence (see §106.45(b)(5)(iii) reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While protecting complainants' privacy (rape-shield), recipients also must ensure parties can gather and present relevant evidence; investigative and evidentiary rules must balance these interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trauma-informed training and careful use of trauma-informed evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: Investigators should receive trauma-informed training so they can avoid re-traumatizing complainants during investigations. This is distinct from a trauma-informed approach to evaluating testimony; use of trauma-informed approaches to evaluating evidence can lead adjudicators to overlook significant inconsistencies, which may be incompatible with due process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must train investigators to avoid re-traumatization, and adjudicators/investigators should use trauma and memory science that is well grounded; noteworthy inconsistencies must be considered and balanced rather than ignored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preference for an adjudicatory model (hearings with decision-makers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ABA Criminal Justice Section Task Force expressed a preference for the 'adjudicatory model,' defined as 'a hearing in which both parties are entitled to be present, evidence is presented, and the decision-maker(s) determine(s) whether a violation of school policy has occurred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commenters and some authorities favor hearings where evidence is tested before a neutral factfinder; institutions should consider this model when designing grievance procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-examination and live hearings concerns
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters and studies discuss that cross-examination can rely on victim-blaming attitudes, sex stereotypes, and rape myths, and that live-, video-, or videotaped-testimony format shows no significant differences in observers' ability to detect deception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rule (discussed elsewhere in the preamble) includes provisions about live hearings with cross-examination for postsecondary recipients; institutions must balance cross-examination rights with concerns about bias and trauma.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decisionmaker impartiality and avoidance of combined investigatory/adjudicative roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisionmakers must make credibility determinations independently and not simply adopt the investigator's findings. Combining investigative and adjudicative functions in a single individual raises serious concerns about fairness and bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law and commenters warn against allowing an investigator to dominate a panel or serve as both prosecutor and tribunal; institutions should structure roles to minimize the risk of actual or perceived bias and allow effective review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training requirement expanded to informal resolution facilitators
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations revise §106.45(b)(1)(iii) to include training for persons who facilitate informal resolution processes, in addition to Title IX Coordinators, investigators, and decision-makers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anyone involved in facilitating informal resolutions must receive appropriate training consistent with the training required for other Title IX personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who may sign/file a formal complaint and complainant autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.30 specifies that only a complainant, or a Title IX Coordinator, can sign or file a formal complaint initiating the grievance process, and clarifies that when a Title IX Coordinator signs a formal complaint that action is not taken 'on behalf of' the complainant; the complainant retains autonomy over filing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Final regulations removed a proposal that would have required Title IX Coordinators to file upon receipt of multiple reports to avoid forcing a formal complaint over a complainant's wishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on informal resolution for employee-on-student allegations
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 106.45(b)(9) does not permit recipients to offer or facilitate informal resolution of allegations that an employee sexually harassed a student.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal resolution can be used for other types of formal complaints (subject to consent), but is categorically disallowed where the respondent is an employee accused of harassing a student.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title IX Coordinator duties regarding supportive measures
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.44(a) requires the Title IX Coordinator promptly to contact each complainant to discuss the availability of supportive measures (with or without a formal complaint), consider the wishes of the complainant with respect to supportive measures, and explain to the complainant the process for filing a formal complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinators must proactively offer and explain supportive measures, respect complainant wishes, and ensure complainants understand procedural options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients may choose whether non-postsecondary grievance processes include hearings, but must describe criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-postsecondary institution recipients' grievance processes may, but need not, provide for a hearing; recipients have flexibility to make hearings available on a case-by-case basis, so long as the grievance process clearly identifies the circumstances under which a hearing may or may not be held and any rules apply equally to both parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A recipient cannot, for example, state that a hearing will be held only if a respondent requests it; it could state a hearing will be held only if both parties request/consent or if the Coordinator determines it is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flexibility in calculating 'days' used in the regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients may choose how to calculate 'days' as used in these final regulations; e.g., a ten-day period may be calendar days, school days, business days, or other method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients must make their chosen method clear in the grievance process so parties understand timelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof rests on the recipient
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the final regulations, §106.45(b)(5)(i), the burden of proof rests on the recipient, not on the parties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions (as the factfinding body) must gather and present sufficient evidence to meet the chosen standard; parties should not be required to bear that burden.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards of evidence and institutional choice
rubrics_metrics.description: A preponderance of the evidence standard means concluding that a fact is more likely than not to be true; a clear and convincing standard means concluding that a fact is highly probable to be true. The standard of evidence chosen should reflect the level of confidence appropriate for the adjudication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department believes recipients' selection of a standard should reflect the institutional judgment about required confidence and should be applied equally to students and employees; different degrees of confidence should not be applied based on respondent status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standards reflect societal judgment about confidence required
rubrics_metrics.description: The standard of evidence used for a class of claims reflects a societal judgment about the level of confidence a decision-maker should have before reaching a conclusion in the case (citing In re Winship).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients should consider the gravity of consequences and societal expectations when choosing their standard and ensure transparency so complainants understand the institution's decision threshold.
